paragraphs: Flock Safety sells license plate readers, video cameras, gunshot detection and response drones to law enforcement agencies, schools, businesses and neighborhoods to help them deter crime, respond to emergencies and investigate safety incidents. Its license plate recognition cameras capture plates and vehicle characteristics such as make, color and body type to generate investigative leads. Responders get an instant alert when a vehicle matches a customer-defined or NCIC hot list. Users include law enforcement agencies, businesses, neighborhoods, apartment complexes, houses of worship and schools.

Beyond plate readers, Flock sells PTZ video cameras for open areas such as parking lots, intersections and parks, and fixed cameras for buildings and city streets. A gunshot and audio detection product verifies gunfire and links each alert with nearby LPR reads and video. Flock DFR, its drone as first responder system, launches a docked drone to the coordinates of a 911 call, LPR hit or gunshot alert and streams live video to officers before they arrive. Solar-powered mobile trailers cover parking lots, retail centers and construction sites, and an optional Alert Response Service puts trained agents on live alerts.

Flock sells on an annual subscription that covers hardware, software, maintenance and support. The company has reduced its recommended default data retention from 30 days to 7 days, which it says applies to new law enforcement customers. Customers control their data and how it is shared, and every search is logged.

The site says calls for service can be cleared without dispatching a unit, so drones clear non-priority calls while agencies focus elsewhere. paragraphs: SoundThinking, Inc., listed on Nasdaq as SSTI, sells AI and data-driven public safety technology to law enforcement, civic leadership, and security professionals. Its ShotSpotter system detects and verifies gunfire incidents in near real time to support awareness and response. ShotSpotter is one part of the SafetySmart Platform, which the company says unifies gunfire alerts, vehicle intelligence, investigations, field awareness, and operational context in one place.

Alongside ShotSpotter, the platform includes CrimeTracer, a law enforcement search engine, and CaseBuilder, an investigation management system. ResourceRouter directs patrol and community anti-violence resources to where they will have the most effect. SafePointe screens entry points in high-traffic environments for weapons. PlateRanger connects vehicle sightings across time, location, and related events for investigators.

The company was founded as ShotSpotter in 1996 by physicist Dr. Robert Showen, who was then locating earthquake epicenters at the Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California. After hearing gunshots in a nearby neighborhood, he applied the sound wave principles from his earthquake research to detecting and locating gunfire. Ralph Clark, hired as CEO in 2010, moved the system to a subscription rather than a capital hardware purchase. He also brought the human review of potential gunshots in-house through a centralized Incident Review Center. The gunshot detection service now serves over 170 cities. In 2023 the company rebranded from ShotSpotter to SoundThinking and launched the SafetySmart Platform. It reports more than 300 customers and work with approximately 2,100 agencies.

paragraphs: LiveView Technologies, known as LVT, sells rapidly deployable security units configured as mobile trailers, wall mounts, or pole mounts. The company says the units are used by DOTs, oil and gas operators, law enforcement, retailers, construction firms, and housing operators. Each mobile unit runs on its own, carrying solar panels, cellular and available satellite connectivity, lighting, a loud speaker, and a configurable selection of cameras. Pole-mounted versions instead take grid power for fixed coverage where infrastructure already exists.

The software side is a cloud platform reached from a phone or desktop, with a forensic search that sorts footage by keywords such as white car or crowd formation. From a mobile device an operator can zoom in, turn on the lights, and start speaker talk downs. A companion app called SafeNow lets employees set off floodlights, strobes, and audio warnings with one swipe.

On the public side, LVT lists remote monitoring of borders, government buildings, parks, school campuses, healthcare facilities, and military sites. The Arcadia Police Department added LVT Units to its operations for surveillance and crime prevention. Prologis put more than 70 LVT Units across industrial real estate properties in multiple states. LVT has been headquartered in Utah since 2005.

paragraphs: Kaiden AI sells AI simulation training software to law enforcement agencies and academies. The product turns an agency's policies and training standards into AI simulations, guided coaching, and evaluations that officers can complete anywhere. Agencies build scenarios, assign practice, and measure officer performance from one platform. The simulations use AI personas meant to cover the full range of people officers encounter in the field.

The company frames the product around the law enforcement training lifecycle. Recruits get more opportunities to practice communication, judgment, articulation, and policy application before the situations evaluated in the FTO program. For serving officers, scenarios cover policy changes, legal updates, emerging threats, and high-risk encounters, with a separate track for interviewing and investigative decision-making. Instructors can assign targeted practice based on documented performance gaps without adding role-player or instructor burden.

Testimonials on the site come from the Baltimore and Atlanta police departments; Lt. Jason Foore of Atlanta says recruits using Kaiden AI felt more confident during practical exercises. A blog post says the Baltimore Police Department has launched a pilot of Kaiden AI at the Baltimore Police Academy for academy and in-service programs. The company reports completing a SOC 2 Type 1 attestation to protect agency and trainee data. A January 2025 post announces a $1M pre-seed round.

brands.name: Simpleview (Granicus Destinations)
brands.description:
Simpleview sells destination-marketing technology and marketing services to the organizations that promote places. Its own homepage now carries the title "Granicus Destinations | Marketing Solutions | CVB Tourism Software" and the line "From small towns to big countries, Granicus Destinations is the tourism software partner to help you engage stakeholders, attract visitors, and win bids for conventions and events." The product menu lists Simpleview CMS, "designed by and for DMOs"; Simpleview CRM, an industry-specific CRM with "seamless integration with more than 20 programs"; Simpleview DAM for digital assets; Destination Canvas; an Online Booking & Referral Engine branded Book > Direct that "lets visitors book directly with your partners and stakeholders"; Partner Engagement & Website Monetization (DTN), which "facilitates targeted advertising on destination websites" so DMOs can earn revenue; user-generated content; mobile apps; digital accessibility; email marketing and automation via Act-On; digital proposals; event management; short-term rental solutions; and a data tier of Simpleview Data Engine, dashboards, pace reporting and a meetings and groups database. Alongside the software it sells agency work: website design, visual identity, SEO, paid media, digital strategy, a Digital Maturity Model, DMO partner engagement, the Digital Influence Report and training. The acquisition release describes the buyers as "convention bureaus, venues, tourism boards, destination marketing organizations, and attractions." Granicus's destinations page states that "more than 500 DMOs use our CMS," that "1,000-plus destinations" use the CRM, and that 400M+ people visit those websites annually.

Both sites confirm Simpleview is part of Granicus, so the careers redirect is corroborated rather than relied on. Granicus's destinations FAQ asks "Is Simpleview now part of Granicus?" and answers "Yes. Simpleview was acquired by Granicus, and the legacy Simpleview products, services, expertise, and thought leadership are now a part of the Granicus portfolio serving destination marketers," then explains the two-site split: the solutions "remain at simpleviewinc.com" during a transition and "The two websites will be combined in the near future." Granicus's own office list gives Tucson, AZ, 8950 N. Oracle Road as "Simpleview, now part of Granicus" - the address in Simpleview's footer. Simpleview's Our Story page says plainly "We were acquired by Granicus." The Granicus press release of September 5, 2024 announced the acquisition, said Simpleview "works with more than 1,000 premier destinations," quoted Simpleview CEO Ryan George, and put the combined company at more than 7,000 organizations and roughly 2,000 employees. A May 5, 2026 release then announced Granicus Destinations as "a dedicated business segment" with its own leadership and the DXC platform, "supporting more than 1,000 destinations worldwide, including all 11 FIFA World Cup host cities." Our Story dates the business to 2001 as 220 Solutions, founded by Ryan George, Bill Simpson and Scott Wood; the first web-based CRM built for DMOs in 2002, with Visit Lauderdale as first client; a 2007 merger with cvbTV at 100 clients; New Media Gateway in 2010; Software Management, Inc. in 2014, adding 92 DMOs; and later 2Synergize, Jackrabbit Systems, Eventsforce and the MINT+ meetings database.

profile_research.description:
Granicus sells cloud software and services that governments use to communicate with the public, publish and stream meetings, run websites and forms, and manage records and permits. Its own site frames the offering as two platforms: the Government Experience Cloud (GXC), split into Service Cloud ("Deliver services without friction"), Engagement Cloud ("Grow and activate audiences") and Operations Cloud ("Automate workflows and reduce costs"), and the Destination Experience Cloud (DXC) for destination marketing. Layered on those are Government Experience Agent (GXA), described as an AI-powered digital agent built for government, a Federal Experience Cloud, and the GXI Enterprise and GXI Foundations intelligence tiers. The solution pages group the underlying products into agenda and meeting management, websites and CMS, digital services and forms, digital communication and engagement, permitting and licensing, and public records and short-term-rental compliance. The product directory names each tool with its legacy brand in parentheses: Communications (govDelivery), Websites & CMS (govAccess, OpenCities, Intranet), Records Request Management (GovQA and GovQA Legal), Short-Term Rentals (Host Compliance), Forms & Workflow (OpenForms), Service Request Management (govService and OneView), Permitting, Compliance & Licensing (AMANDA and SmartGov), Land & Official Records (govRecords), Sentiment & Feedback (EngagementHQ), Video (self-managed, and Swagit partially and fully managed), Boards and Commissions, and agenda management under the Legistar, OneMeeting and Peak names. The buyers named under "Who we serve" are local government, state government, federal government, education, special districts, elected officials and destinations, with country sites for Canada, the United Kingdom, Australia & New Zealand, India, and Latin America & the Caribbean. Granicus also sells consulting and digital agency work through the Granicus Experience Group (GXG).

Granicus is the parent of this family rather than a member of one. Its company page states "more than 2,000 employees across the globe supporting more than 7,000 public sector organizations," and the careers page repeats "about 2,000 of us" spread across "eight countries" in a remote-first workplace; that page's "Explore roles" button points at careers-granicus.icims.com, the iCIMS board the Simpleview careers page also lands on. The homepage figure block claims 7,000+ public sector customers, 360M people in the Granicus subscriber network, 100% of U.S. federal cabinet-level agencies, 48 of the 50 largest U.S. cities, 30B digital experiences and 22B government messages delivered annually, 8B government website views, 3.5M online forms submitted, 2M record requests served and 123K government meetings streamed each year. The company page carries a timeline headed "Organic and inorganic growth through best-in-class acquisitions": Granicus and GovDelivery were independently founded in 1999 and merged in 2017; Vision Internet arrived in 2018; a London-based government service provider in 2019; Bang the Table, OpenCities and GovQA in 2021 alongside Australia/New Zealand expansion; a full-service video provider and a government CRM in 2022 with entry into Latin America and the Caribbean; Simpleview in 2024; and GXA's launch in 2025. The same page names Vista Equity Partners as an existing investor joined by Harvest Partners in 2020. The trust-center office list gives Denver, Washington DC, Tucson, Ottawa, London, Melbourne, Auckland, San Juan and Bengaluru.

paragraphs: RollKall sells an off-duty work management platform with separate experiences for law enforcement agencies, officers, and the clients who hire them. Agencies post off-duty jobs with requirements and compliance rules, and officers are matched based on eligibility, availability, and department policy. Invoices are generated from clock-in and clock-out data, payments are routed to officers, and 1099s are handled digitally. An agency can run the platform itself or have RollKall run it as a managed service.

Officers use a mobile app to browse available shifts, view pay rates and locations, accept jobs, and clock in and out from their phones. Payment options include WeeklyPay, PrePay, and InstantPay, which lets officers access earnings immediately after completing a job. Clients and vendors request officers through a branded client portal with approval workflows, automated invoicing, and electronic payment processing. The company reports 85%+ officer adoption within the first 30 days across its deployments.

Published case studies cover the Irving Police Department and the Paulding County Sheriff's Office. Testimonials on the site come from the Cincinnati Police Department, the Prince George's County Police Department, the Randall County Sheriff's Office, and the St. Charles County Police Department.

paragraphs: CentralSquare Technologies sells software to public agencies, from dispatch centers to city halls. On the public safety side, its suite runs from computer aided dispatch and NG911 call handling through to jail management and analytics. On the administration side, the company says public administrators in over 8,000 communities use it for finance, HR, payroll, asset management, permitting and tax collection.

Public Safety Suite Enterprise connects 911, CAD, RMS, Mobile and Jail in a single platform. A version called Public Safety Suite Pro is designed for small and mid-sized agencies that want one vendor rather than several systems. Vertex NG911 Call Handling gives 911 centers a single platform for voice, text, video and caller location. Vertex also carries built-in text translation and transcription for more than 150 languages, which the company says runs in under 10 seconds. The company says it secures cloud data against cyberattacks through a partnership with Amazon Web Services.

The homepage counts more than 8,000 agencies nationwide as customers. Customers named on the site include the California Highway Patrol. Case studies include the Edgar County 911 team, whose partnership with CentralSquare serves a community of 16,000 residents. Morgan County 911 in Alabama is featured for upgrading to Vertex NG911 Call Handling.

paragraphs: Niche Technology sells NicheRMS365, a records management system for police agencies, which use it to share information and eliminate siloed systems. The company says the system captures every aspect of policing from the front line to the courtroom. It describes the product as designed for multi-agency use and calls large projects its specialty.

Sworn officers in over 180 agencies worldwide use NicheRMS365. Recent announcements on the site include South Yorkshire Police, which plans to implement NicheRMS365 to modernize crime recording and strengthen data integrity. Durham Constabulary and Warwickshire Police have each selected the system as a platform that centralizes operational data. The Toronto Police Service chose it as its records management system. Orange County, New York won a 2025 Government Experience Award from the Center for Digital Government for its NicheRMS project.

Founded in 1992, Niche Technology is a private Canadian corporation based in Winnipeg, Manitoba, with additional offices in Canada, the United States and the United Kingdom. It is wholly owned by its founders, who remain active in day-to-day operations. In the United States, NicheRMS365 is available to federal agencies through the General Services Administration Information Technology Schedule 70. It is also offered through the New York State Umbrella Contract and the Dell National Government Contract.

paragraphs: FaceTec sells face verification software that organizations use to confirm a remote user is real and physically present, both at account onboarding and on later logins. Its products cover 3D liveness checks, KYC and 3D face verification, running from an ordinary 2D camera rather than infrared hardware. During onboarding the software records a quick video selfie, verifies 3D liveness, matches the resulting 3D FaceMap to the photo on the ID and checks the ID for signs of tampering. When the user returns, a new video selfie is compared with the stored FaceMap, and a high match, which FaceTec rates at 1/125M FAR, can grant account access.

FaceTec has run a Spoof Bounty Program since October 2019 and says it has passed Ingenium, Bixelab, Praetorian and iBeta Testing Lab Level 1-5 PAD and IAD testing with 0% FAR. The bounty currently stands at $600,000. The company's stated best practice is for customers to keep users' biometric data, as 3D FaceMap or 3D FaceVector records, on their own servers, which run FaceTec's software inside the customer's firewall.

A related product, UR Codes, carries digitally signed biometric data so a codeholder can prove legal identity and age both in person and remotely. FaceTec says it trained its 3D algorithms with the help of over half a million volunteer testers from over 180 countries. It lists more than 90 channel partners worldwide.

paragraphs: SkySafe sells a drone detection and airspace intelligence platform that gives businesses the visibility and forensic detail to identify drone activity in real time and build legally sound cases when incidents occur. The company states the platform detects 96% of drone models, including drones flying without active signals. It can pinpoint where a drone took off, where it landed and the location of its controller. Alerts go out through SMS, Microsoft Teams, Slack, CommandCentral Aware or an existing ops stack. The platform produces forensic reports intended for law enforcement or federal agencies.

One case study describes how a near-miss drone flight over a crowd of 10,000 at Fort Adams State Park led Rhode Island toward a statewide drone detection strategy. The University of Illinois Police Department used SkySafe to monitor and respond to drone activity across campus events and facilities, and the University of Louisiana at Monroe uses it to separate authorized university flights from unauthorized activity.

Press releases on its site describe the product as a cloud-based SaaS platform providing real-time and historical drone data to help distinguish unauthorized drones from authorized ones. In November 2025 it launched Forensics as a Service, which the company says lets agencies and organizations respond to and investigate drone incidents on their own. CEO Grant Jordan served as an officer in the US Air Force for four years after graduating from MIT and was President of Somerset Recon.

paragraphs: Robin Radar Systems makes 360 degree, 3D radar systems that detect, track and classify small flying objects such as birds, bats and drones. It sells them to aviation, defence, security and ecology teams that want a full view of their airspace. Its two main products are IRIS, a 3D drone radar in a 29 kg package, and MAX, a 3D bird detection radar.

IRIS uses micro-doppler classification and deep neural network technology to distinguish blades and rotating parts. It combines 360 degree views, 60 degree elevation and a 5 km instrumented range. A software-only update, Long-Range Mode, lets operators switch between 5 km and 12 km instrumented ranges in minutes. MAX pairs with two software interfaces, Bird Viewer for live airspace and Report Viewer for historical analysis. Airports, airfields and wind farms use the bird and bat radars to react to hazards as they emerge.

The name comes from a 1980 project by the Dutch research institute TNO to prevent bird strikes on Royal Netherlands Air Force planes. Siete Hamminga, now CEO, spun the technology out of TNO in 2010 to found the company. It reports more than 300 radars deployed worldwide and a staff of 150 or more people. In 2024 its shareholders reached an acquisition agreement with the Dutch investment company Parcom. Scarecrow, a maker of bird dispersal and data logging systems based on bio-acoustic technology, is a Robin company.

paragraphs: Lexipol sells policy manuals, training, wellness resources, performance reporting, and grant support to public safety agencies, delivered through one system. Its buyers are the people running those agencies, from fire and police chiefs to risk managers, dispatch supervisors, and city administrators. An agency can begin with a single product, such as Policy or Wellness, and add others as it goes.

The policy product is the core: state-specific manuals researched and written by policy and legal professionals, then kept current as laws and standards change. Personnel acknowledge each policy electronically, which creates an audit trail for accreditation, audits, or legal reviews. Daily Training Bulletins turn those policies into practice through short scenario-based lessons. The LexOne platform ties training assignments to policy, warns leaders when licenses or credentials are about to expire, and tracks the data agencies need for reporting. Online courses carry accreditation from organizations such as IADLEST, POST, and CAPCE.

Lexipol was created in 2003 by two attorneys who were also former law enforcement officers. Co-founder Gordon Graham still records a weekly two-minute video tip for public safety and local government personnel. The company says its wellness product alone supports more than 1,000 agencies across the U.S. and Canada. Among the chiefs quoted on the site, Edward Delmore of the Gulf Shores (AL) Police Department compares a subscription to having another full-time administrator assigned to policy.

quote.text: We help public safety agencies and municipalities operate at the highest standards.

paragraphs: AlliConnect sells wellness software to public safety agencies that runs peer support teams, check-ins, referrals and clinical connection in one confidential system of record. Its therapist network is pitched as something other than a directory: therapists who understand the work, matched to the person on a guaranteed timeline. That timeline is scheduling within 24 hours and a first appointment within one week. The site puts the vetted clinician network at over 1,200.

Dashboards connect to a department's CAD and RMS, so critical incident types and cumulative exposure trigger workflows automatically and the data comes back anonymized for reporting. Brief, confidential check-ins cover six domains of wellness, and any risk they identify is routed to the wellness team rather than to command. A custom resource center holds the department's own programs, contacts and links rather than a generic wellness library.

Colleen Hilton, a licensed Marriage and Family Therapist who has spent more than 20 years working with police officers, firefighters, paramedics, 911 dispatchers and corrections, founded the company. A testimonial on the home page from S. Ryckman of the Bellingham Fire Department calls AlliConnect a pillar of that organization's peer support and responder wellness program. In April 2024 the company announced an officer wellness program with the Hartselle Police Department. Its trust page lists HIPAA compliance and data protection.

paragraphs: ForceMetrics sells Velocity, a search and analytics platform for public safety agencies that pulls CAD, RMS and other records systems into one search covering people, locations, vehicles and events. Officers, analysts and command staff get structured records, narratives and unstructured content back in under a second, with filters that surface connections across CAD, RMS, JMS and regional data.

A universal data model links not only an agency's current systems of record but multiple generations of those systems, so historical and current information is searchable together. Flow Static unlocks data from legacy CAD and RMS systems, and Flow Historical adds e-citations, crash reports, court data and EMS records. Flexible Person Merge combines person records from across the agency and multiple jurisdictions into a single enriched profile, and users can merge or unmerge at any time as new information arrives.

For command staff, FMStat replaces rigid CompStat packets with real-time dashboards that show crime trends and what is driving them. Horizon AI summarizes large volumes of reports and spots patterns across related incidents, with every connection pointing back to the records behind it, inside what the company calls a CJIS-compliant environment. Agencies named on the home page include High Point, NC, New Castle County, DE and Beverly Hills, CA. The company describes its team as veteran law enforcement officials who built the tools they wished they had in the field.

paragraphs: ECINS sells a license-free cloud system for collaborative case management, built for agencies that coordinate support for vulnerable people. Its case management module is used by tens of thousands of users in the UK, including police, health and councils. The central idea is a single shared record, so a client does not repeat the same information to every agency involved. The company reports results across the UK, the United States and Australia.

Work usually begins in the referral module, which replaces paper forms with secure online forms that clients and practitioners fill in themselves. Once a referral is approved, its information can be transferred into the case management module. Within case management, staff receive alerts for significant activity such as child protection interventions. They can also track commonalities between individuals through search fields such as addresses, vehicle license plates and educational institutions. A client engagement module and a MyPortal app let clients receive reminders, respond to messages and tasks, and ask questions from their phones.

Beyond casework, a community collaboration module lets residents, neighbourhood watch groups, business communities, police and local authorities work together on detailed neighbourhood profiles. A staff tasking and oversight module is described as still in development. The homepage claims thousands of users across multiple countries. The system is sold license-free to encourage wide participation at no extra cost.

paragraphs: D-Fend Solutions sells counter-drone systems to military, law enforcement and homeland security agencies. Its core product, EnforceAir, detects a rogue drone, takes control of it through a radio-frequency cyber takeover and brings it to a safe landing. The company describes the approach as non-kinetic and AI-enhanced, built for sensitive and challenging environments.

EnforceAir can operate autonomously or under manual control, and it detects, locates and identifies rogue drones in a protected airspace before taking them over. It is sold in several deployment packages, including a Homeland Security & Law Enforcement Bundle and two tactical configurations, EnforceAir PLUS and EnforceAir2. EnforceAir PLUS, launched in August 2025, adds radar and a jammer to the RF-cyber layer. Beyond agencies, the company says the system has been chosen for large-scale events at stadiums, arenas and open-air venues and for VIP protection.

In an August 2026 press release the company says EnforceAir provided counter-drone security across World Cup host cities and was adopted by more than 20 public safety agencies. Chairman and CEO Zohar Halachmi co-founded the company after founding two mobile and enterprise application start-ups. Its U.S. arm, D-Fend Solutions AD, Inc., is located in McLean, Virginia. In June 2026 the company announced an agreement to be acquired by Motorola Solutions. Its newsroom now states that it has officially joined Motorola Solutions.

paragraphs: Sentrycs makes counter-drone systems that detect, track, identify and mitigate unauthorized drones for defense, homeland security and critical infrastructure environments. Rather than radar, it uses passive RF cyber technology to pick up drone communication signals and locate both the drone and its operator. Detection reports the drone type, serial number and operator position. Mitigation does not jam the drone; the system takes control of it through a cyber takeover. If required, it integrates with other types of effector, including jammers.

The company says a team of communications and radio frequency experts embarked in 2017 on developing modular solutions that could be tailored to each customer's drone environment. The system is built for complex and urban environments, where it aims to minimize interference with surrounding communications. It says its customers include governments, security forces and critical infrastructure operators worldwide. Its blog is aimed partly at law enforcement, with posts on how to legally take down a rogue drone and on lessons from recent UAS attacks.

On November 18th, 2025, Ondas Holdings Inc. (NASDAQ:ONDS) announced it had completed the acquisition of Sentrycs. The announcement describes the company as Sentry CS Ltd., based in Israel. It puts Sentrycs at approximately 200 deployments across six continents in more than 25 countries.

paragraphs: Ekin Smart City Technology sells monitoring devices and software that law enforcement agencies use to enforce the laws of their communities. The product list runs from an Automatic License Plate Reader, or ALPR, to red light enforcement and speed and traffic enforcement. All of those devices feed data captured at the edge to maestro, the company's backend platform, which analyzes it in real time. Violations can then be issued automatically and monitored from a central dashboard.

One product, Ekin Patrol G2, is a modular AI-powered bar that attaches to vehicles, so a patrol car carries the sensors instead of fixed infrastructure. The company says it can detect and process speeding and parking violations in real time. It can also alert officers when someone approaches the vehicle. Ekin markets similar monitoring to neighborhoods, where the systems watch vehicles, pedestrian traffic and large wildlife around the clock in all weather.

Ekin designs and manufactures its own hardware and develops its software in-house. It states that it has used machine learning and artificial intelligence for more than 15 years. Both the law enforcement and neighborhood pages point to a case study of Coral Gables, Florida. A December 2025 press headline announces a $25M U.S. expansion and a transition to U.S.-based manufacturing.

paragraphs: Flash AI builds investigative software in Ohio for law enforcement agencies. Its main product, Flash PD, takes an entire caseload of video, audio, images, documents and phone extractions into one unified system. Flash PD accepts 115+ file types and processes them in parallel. Investigators then ask questions in plain language and get direct answers with linked source evidence and timestamps.

A second product, Flash Signal, connects to a correctional facility's call recording system so recorded inmate calls flow in as they happen, or historical libraries can be uploaded in batch. Each call is transcribed and scored low, medium or high risk from its content, language and behavioral signals, so investigators open the high-risk calls first. The company says a 60-day pilot at a correctional facility identified 33,004 high-risk signals with zero manual review hours required.

A third product, Flash Chat, extends private AI chat and document analysis to the rest of an agency, with a free trial for the standard deployment and CJIS deployments available by demo. Flash AI states that queries, uploads and conversations are never used to train AI models, and that hosting is on AWS infrastructure in the United States. The customers page lists Whitehall Police Department and Perry Township Police Department as active deployments, and Muskingum County and Guernsey County sheriff's offices as previous pilots.

paragraphs: nexSOS connects citizens and public safety agencies through real-time incident reporting, location sharing, and NOAA weather alerts, backed by a government portal. Citizens use a mobile app to share their GPS location with emergency contacts and first responders, record video reports with the phone's camera, and call emergency services directly. The company stresses that the app is not a 911 replacement.

Incident reports are stored and routed to a backend portal where public safety agencies filter, review, and monitor incidents across their jurisdiction. Agencies can filter by region, timestamp and category, review video, and see NOAA alerts alongside citizen reports in one view. The page names Emergency Management Offices, County Dispatch Centers and Municipal Safety Agencies as the users it is built for. The pitch to them is early incident context before or alongside 911 calls.

Government access is licensed annually by jurisdiction size, with a base tier of unlimited citizen users, portal access and 12 months of data retention, and larger tiers adding analytics, heat mapping and extended retention. Qualified agencies can start with a 90-day paid pilot that includes full platform access, onboarding support and a usage summary report. nexSOS says the platform originally launched and ran quietly in production and is now being rebuilt as v2, with modernized infrastructure, user experience and government-facing capabilities.

Job distribution runs through a fairness engine that applies the agency's own policies so that each officer gets a fair shot at working jobs. Notifications and job reminders go out automatically, in place of the manual emails, texts and calls a coordinator would otherwise send. As a detail runs, the agency and the business that hired the officers can see when officers are en route, on site and finished. Officers record what happens during a detail in a paperless activity log. Agencies, officers and employers can then pull reports on finances and assignments. The homepage also lists a payment platform among the features.

Detail Kommander was founded by a retired Chief, and it says it builds for law enforcement agencies of all sizes. The company says hundreds of agencies have moved to the software. paragraphs: DefendEye sells autonomous drones to first responders, emergency services and private security teams. A second product category is aimed at tactical, defense and government buyers. The pitch is situational awareness in seconds, an AI-powered search for people on the ground, and a drone that anyone can operate.

There is no pilot and no joystick: the operator controls the drone from a phone and launches it with a single tap. The company says deployment takes under 20 seconds through a single-button activation. Once airborne, the onboard AI locates and tags people so that officers can concentrate on the rescue. Listed flight times run up to 30 minutes on one model and up to 40 minutes on another. One version launches automatically when motion sensors detect activity and returns to land in its box. Missions can be run remotely from any location through the DefendEye Cloud platform.

The company describes itself as a technology company focused on making aerial intelligence faster, simpler and more accessible. It says its systems can support emergency response, public safety, maritime operations and industrial environments. A media section on the about page lists an August 2026 PR Newswire item about an investment led by NovaCapital to scale production. Another item there announces the integration of Starlink Mini into its tube-launched search drone. Earlier coverage listed on the same page describes the drone as the work of a Polish technology company.

paragraphs: Auror sells a retail crime intelligence platform to retailers and law enforcement agencies, built to bring crime intelligence together across a network of both. Retailers capture events in the platform, connect the dots between stores and cases, and identify potential threats.

Auror Core comprises five modules: Intel for incident reporting, Connect the Dots for AI-assisted person of interest matching with human verification, Investigate for case management, Insights for analytics and Audit for compliance workflows. Reported incidents build into in-depth profiles of the people and vehicles affecting an organization. Investigators then use that intel to build, collaborate on and resolve cases. A Risk Detection add-on extends this to prevention, with automatic alerts when known vehicles of interest enter a location. For law enforcement, the Retail Crime Hub, designed by Auror and Axon, moves packaged evidence from retailers straight into Axon Evidence for intake.

Auror puts its network at more than 85,000 stores and more than 3,500 law enforcement agencies, with a decade of accumulated intelligence across them. Auror says Cosentino's Food Stores achieved a 346% return on investment and a reduction of more than 90% in reporting time with the platform. The company has set itself the goal of reducing retail crime by 50% over the next five years.

paragraphs: GovWorx sells CommsCoach, an AI-powered software platform that emergency communications centers use to hire, train, evaluate and support 9-1-1 telecommunicators. It is aimed at the ECC leaders responsible for improving the performance of 9-1-1 professionals. Its modules follow a telecommunicator from candidate through career, linking HIRE, TRAIN, QA and ASSIST in one system, with PROMOTE added for choosing supervisors.

CommsCoach HIRE measures aptitude, resilience, accuracy and composure through structured testing and AI-supported scoring, with tests run onsite or remotely. QA automatically pulls every eligible call and radio transmission, matches transcripts to CAD event data and scores them against the agency's own policies. During live calls, ASSIST listens, transcribes and prompts the call-taker with the policy-specific questions the situation requires. PROMOTE is an evidence-based assessment that identifies leadership potential in supervisor candidates and pairs each result with a personalized development pathway.

An emergency communications administrator at the O'Fallon Police Department in Missouri is quoted saying call-taking compliance rose from single digits to 96% with ASSIST, APCO guidecards and complete QA. In June 2026 APCO International and GovWorx announced a partnership to bring APCO's communications protocols into CommsCoach ASSIST. In August 2026 GovWorx added NEAL, an adaptive non-emergency call handling tool that escalates to a human telecommunicator whenever judgment is needed.

paragraphs: Kodex sells a portal for processing subpoenas and other legal data requests, built for the companies that receive them. Those buyers manage requests from law enforcement through one centralized platform that Kodex says protects both compliance obligations and user privacy. The platform verifies every agent, encrypts every exchange, and keeps a complete record of how each request happened, and the company says requests close in days instead of weeks when both sides work in one system.

Compliance requirements become automated intake forms that catch issues before they start, and a dashboard shows request status, deadlines, and team responses. A single workspace replaces scattered email threads, so a team can work on each request internally and with government agents. Transparency reports generate in seconds, which Kodex pitches as preparation for audits and questions from regulators. Kodex describes itself as the only data request portal used by more than 15,000 government agencies.

Kodex was founded in 2020 in Boston by former FBI counterterrorism agent Matt Donahue. The company says its verification systems stop thousands of fake law enforcement requests, protecting the integrity of legitimate ones. A Coinbase vice president is quoted calling Kodex a partner when engaging with regulators. Bitget's chief compliance officer is also quoted. The feature list ends with SOC2, GDPR, and PCI compliance.

description: AI investigations platform for law enforcement - exhibited at IACP 2026

competitors.why: AI investigative intelligence over case evidence and jail calls with CJIS-compliant AI chat, sold to the same detective bureau.
AI fusing video, phone extractions and jail calls into case timelines for the same investigator buyer weighing an AI investigations tool.

paragraphs: Longeye sells an AI-powered investigative workspace that law enforcement agencies use to analyze digital evidence. An investigator uploads video, audio, phone extractions, social media exports, financial records, and images, then asks questions in plain language. Every answer links back to the exact moment in a video, recording, message, or image, so a finding can be checked later.

Audio and video are transcribed and translated, with searchable transcripts across Spanish, Mandarin, and 99+ more. Each call then lands on a timeline color-coded by relevancy so the conversations most likely to matter come first. A map view plots GPS tracker pings, Cellebrite extraction data, CDR lat/long, and ALPR hits, with a slider that animates movement over time. A standalone product, Longeye Monitor, applies the same engine to jail call review for corrections agencies and jail facilities.

Longeye says it is deployed across the country, from major metropolitan departments and state bureaus of investigation to corrections intelligence units running jail call analysis. Chief Darrell Lowe of the Redmond Police Department is quoted crediting it with closing gaps in a cold-case homicide. On security, the company states it is SOC 2 Type II certified, isolates evidence per agency on dedicated US infrastructure, and never uses evidence to train a large language model. Longeye has raised $5M in seed funding led by Andreessen Horowitz's American Dynamism Fund.

competitors.why: AI video, audio and document redaction (CaseGuard Studio) for the same police records and public disclosure unit

paragraphs: Pimloc sells Secure Redact, an automated system for the bulk redaction of personal data from video. It is aimed at private and public organizations that want to automate data privacy compliance while still getting operational value from their video. Customers use it to process video for data subject access requests and freedom of information requests.

The system's models recognize identifiers such as faces, heads and license plates the way a human observer would, then redact and classify them automatically. It can be applied selectively, removing some or all faces or all vehicle registration details, and it is trained to perform on low-definition CCTV footage. Pimloc states that Secure Redact detects and anonymizes over 99% of identifiable PII in security video. It also says redaction with its AI runs 200 times faster than doing the job by hand.

The company says its capabilities are deployed across transport, public safety, telehealth, insurance, retail, policing and local government. A second product, Pholio, classifies visual content, and Pimloc has used it to evaluate automated detection of online harms. Founders Simon Randall, the CEO, and James Leigh, the CTO, co-created the Autographer wearable image capture device at a previous business, and the privacy challenges of always-on capture led them to start Pimloc.

quote.text: Automated anonymization is the only way to keep up with changing privacy legislation and to responsibly unlock the value of aggregated video data for business operations.

brands.name: NextRec (formerly PerfectMind)
brands.description:
PerfectMind is the former name of the product now sold as nextRec, and nextrec.com keeps a page for it that opens "PerfectMind Software is now nextRec". That page defines the product as "a frictionless, all-in-one recreation management software designed for government agencies and private recreation facilities", and says PerfectMind "serves parks and recreation organizations, martial arts studios, higher-education recreation centers, swim schools, homeowner associations, and facilities offering classes and camps to their community members". The government function is the registration-and-facilities back office of a parks and recreation department: online and on-site registration for "courses, private lessons, drop ins", an "intelligent conflict manager" for scheduling community events, one-time and recurring facility rentals with customizable contract templates and digital customer signatures, point of sale for memberships and passes, built-in email marketing so departments do not sync to outside software, and real-time reporting across "any object or table in your database". A Citywide POS module is offered to consolidate payments across a municipality. The brand still has live surfaces: the knowledge base and user community on nextrec.com both sit at community.perfectmind.com, and the PCI DSS certificate the site links to is filed as "PerfectMind PCI DSS Certificate".

The page gives the family history plainly. "PerfectMind was founded in 1998." "PerfectMind's software was acquired by Xplor Technologies in 2020. In 2022, PerfectMind rebranded to become nextRec." On what changed: "The PerfectMind software platform remains built and powered by the same team - aside from changing its name to nextRec the only change is that PerfectMind software is now part of a global ecosystem with powerful backing, integrations, and support." That answers the "why does this one exist" question differently from its siblings: PerfectMind is not a separate product sitting beside nextRec, it is the same product under its previous name, kept addressable because agencies bought it under that name. The same page says "Xplor Technologies is the parent company of PerfectMind" and that Xplor "serves over 140 markets globally, 75,000 customers daily, and employs over 2,000 Xplorers across the globe". One conflict is worth recording rather than resolving: nextrec.com says PerfectMind was founded in 1998, while Xplor's corporate site says "Founded in 1988, NextRec". Both are the family's own materials and they disagree; neither was treated as settled here.

brands.name: ePACT
brands.description:
ePACT Network sells emergency and health forms automation, described on its homepage as "Emergency and health forms automation that integrates seamlessly with rec management systems" and on its parks and recreation page as a way for "rec leaders to collect, manage and access health & emergency information, waivers and consent forms - all in one secure, compliant platform". The government function is narrow and specific: it is the participant-paperwork layer under a parks and recreation department's programs. The site lists what it collects - "emergency forms with contact information and instructions, medical forms, waivers, consent forms, and personal health and safety needs", plus immunization records, medication authorization forms, allergies, dietary restrictions, medical history and signed consent forms. Named capabilities are configurable eForms, online and offline access, multi-channel communications, search, filtering and reporting, API integration, and paperless check-in and check-out with a "tailorable contact pick up list" for who may collect a child. Buyers named on the site are parks and recreation departments, YMCAs, camps and JCCs, schools, and sports associations. Public-sector customers quoted by name include the City of Kettering, OH, the San Francisco Recreation & Park Department, CA, the City of Newton Parks & Recreation, MA, the Town of Cary, NC, and the Deerfield Park District, IL. On compliance the site claims SOC II Type 2, HIPAA in the US, and PIPA, PIPEDA and FOIPPA in Canada, hosted on Microsoft Azure. Families use it free, storing a "Private Personal Emergency Record (PPER)".

ePACT sits differently in the family from the other brands: it is not a system of record for registration, it is the forms layer that attaches to one. Its own site says it integrates "with your existing registration system, like ActiveNet, Daxko, RecTrac (and more!)" - RecTrac being the sibling Vermont Systems product, ActiveNet and Daxko being competitors of the family. That is the answer to why it exists alongside three registration platforms: it is sold across all of them, including rivals. Its distribution runs through associations rather than the Xplor brand - it is "Exclusive Partner of the NRPA" with member discounts, a "Preferred vendor of the YMCA of the USA", and an "Emergency-supplies partner with the Canadian Red Cross". The family tie is real but quiet: the site footer reads "2026 ePACT Network | All Rights Reserved", with no Xplor copyright, yet it carries an Xplor Recreation logo image linking to cehrecreation.com, and ePACT is not one of the four brands listed on Xplor's own Xplor Recreation page. Its origin is on its about page: ePACT was inspired by a friend, Ayumi, separated from her two daughters during the 2011 earthquake and tsunami in Japan, and unable to learn they were safe for a full day.

brands.name: RecDesk
brands.description:
recdesk.com could not be read. Both the apex and www forms answer a plain fetch with an HTTP 202 and a Sucuri interstitial, and a real browser is served a "Robot Challenge Screen" that did not clear on repeated attempts. No attempt was made to defeat it, so nothing below comes from RecDesk's own site. What follows is from Xplor's corporate site, which is the family's own material. Xplor writes: "Founded in 2005, RecDesk provides scalable, easy-to-use software for parks and recreation departments, aquatic centers, schools, community centers, HOAs, and small municipalities. Its integrations with access control, GIS/address databases, and financial systems help teams streamline facility scheduling, program management, and operational workflows - reducing manual effort and system fragmentation." Xplor adds that "Business and community leaders can run more efficient programs, offer better resident experiences, and make data-driven decisions that strengthen their community services."

RecDesk is one of the four brands Xplor lists on its Xplor Recreation page, alongside Vermont Systems, NextRec and CampBrain, and Xplor's "Visit RecDesk" link points to recdesk.com. The distinction Xplor's own wording draws between the siblings is the size and type of buyer: RecDesk is described for "small municipalities", aquatic centers and HOAs, where Vermont Systems is described for "municipal, county, state, and federal military recreation organizations". RecDesk's postings run through the Rippling board shared across this family, clubessential-holdings-cjb, which also carries an asset named Xplor_Logo_withTag_Color.png. Beyond that, this record is deliberately short. Anything further about RecDesk's product, customers or scale would have to be invented, because its site refused to be read.

paragraphs: EFORCE Software sells web-based software to law enforcement agencies, built to raise productivity and improve record quality. It also offers tools for corrections staff, which the company says were built by corrections staff. A further set of tools serves municipal courts. The company says it built its own suite of web-based software from the ground up on the idea that law enforcement software should be advanced but easy to use.

EFORCE has served the law enforcement industry since 2003. It says it was the first to deliver a suite of browser-based solutions of this kind. The stated goal is to reduce time spent in the office so officers get back to the field. More than 20% of its employees have been Patrol Officers, Detectives, Dispatchers, Jailers or Administrators.

The homepage says agencies of all sizes from across the country use the software. Testimonials there are attributed to agencies including the Jacksonville Police Department. One of those testimonials singles out the software being web-based and accessible from anywhere. The company counts more than 20 years designing and implementing software for public safety agencies.

paragraphs: CivicEye sells cloud software for law enforcement and prosecutors, pitched as a way to improve daily workflows and community outcomes. The platform has three main products: a records management system for police called CivicRMS, prosecutor case management called CivicCase, and judicial document management called CivicDocs. A fourth, CivicCase for Courts, is aimed at judges and clerks in municipal courts.

CivicRMS creates NIBRS-compliant reports from incident reports, and its validation tools track errors and point to fixes. Integrations with dispatch and jail systems let officers pull dispatch calls, incident details, arrest records and inmate data without leaving the RMS. CivicDocs holds digital evidence and generates audit logs that track the chain of custody between the arresting agency and the prosecutor's office. Users reach the system through role-based portals for prosecutors, clerks, law enforcement and defense attorneys.

The company traces its start to 2007, when it built software for police departments in upstate New York under the name J2 Software and later Agisent Technologies. It is now based in Charlotte, North Carolina, and says it has deployed its software to over 95 public safety and criminal justice agencies across the country. It also says its prosecutor software is used across Tennessee, where the entire Tennessee District Attorney General's Conference adopted it.

paragraphs: BriefCam sells video analytics software that makes recorded surveillance video searchable, actionable and quantifiable. Its patented VIDEO SYNOPSIS technology condenses hours of surveillance into a short summary by overlaying multiple events, each tagged with its original timestamp, onto a single frame that users can filter by object type and attributes. The software is camera-agnostic, integrates with video management systems such as XProtect, and also works as a standalone solution for agencies that only need file-based review.

Three modules, Review, Respond and Research, are used respectively for post-incident search, real-time alerts and quantifying data trends. Every customer needs Review as a base and can then add Respond, Research or both. License plate recognition works on any camera, with no need for dedicated LPR licenses per camera. For commercial users, people counting tracks queues and crowd movement and measures occupancy to improve space use and traffic flow.

BriefCam serves law enforcement, transportation, retail and more, across public and private sectors. Customer stories on the site cover Tlaxcala, Mexico, Villa El Salvador and the City of Hartford's real-time crime center. The site is published by Milestone Systems, which lists BriefCam among its products alongside the XProtect video management software.

paragraphs: NiCE sells Evidencentral, a cloud-based digital evidence management platform for public safety and justice agencies. The platform is meant to manage data from the moment an incident happens until a case is closed and prosecuted. For emergency communications centers that means incident recording and reconstruction, voice-to-text transcription, quality assurance and coaching, and PSAP performance reporting.

NiCE Inform automates incident reconstruction, evidence production, quality assurance and real-time performance metrics reporting. NiCE Investigate then brings evidence and associated information to investigators, patrol officers and criminal justice partners, with the stated aim of breaking down information silos. Further along the process, NiCE Justice and NiCE Defense help prosecution, defense and courts manage growing volumes of digital evidence. An Evidencentral Marketplace of technology vendors is designed to make it simpler and faster for emergency communications, law enforcement and criminal justice agencies to bring evidence together.

A customer story on the page comes from British Transport Police, attributed to its Senior Project Management for Digital Policing. The company describes the platform as powered by artificial intelligence and offers demos through the site.

paragraphs: Babel Street sells risk intelligence software to national defense and law enforcement agencies, global enterprises and FinTech companies. Its platform combines rights-cleared global data, governed AI agents and Insights Investigator, its investigation interface. Through that interface analysts submit queries in natural language and receive entity relationships, hidden ownership flags, foreign influence signals and cited evidence. The data behind it spans more than 200 languages, with AI trained to catch slang and coded language that translation alone misses.

For law enforcement, the company says the platform helps agencies investigate and prevent increasingly complex criminal activity. Analysts and police use it to detect early warning signs and uncover behavioral patterns in public data. The identity products process millions of names against watchlists, with matching behavior tuned to reduce false positives and negatives. Border security agencies use the same tools to flag high-risk travelers, cargo and networks.

Its vendor risk product is delivered as secure SaaS or API and embeds continuous monitoring into procurement workflows. Babel Street says a large majority of U.S. national security agencies use it. paragraphs: Chainalysis sells blockchain intelligence software that investigators and compliance teams use to investigate illicit activity, manage risk exposure and prevent fraud. Its investigation product, Reactor, is used by law enforcement, intelligence, regulatory and tax agencies, crypto exchanges, financial institutions, and corporate investigation teams. The company says its intelligence is relied on by more than 1,500 organizations worldwide and has been proven in landmark cases.

Reactor traces funds across 27+ blockchains, 40M+ assets, 325M+ swaps, and 300+ bridges and DEXs. For investigators without blockchain expertise, a companion product called Rapid takes any crypto address and reveals wallet ownership, balances, and where funds came from and went. When a recovery seed turns up in a search or arrest, Wallet Scan checks it across 45+ wallets, 15+ blockchains including privacy coins, and 100+ million addresses per seed. Reactor can run in the cloud, on-premises, or in FedRAMP-certified environments.

Customer stories on the site include BNY, described as the world's largest custodian bank, which chose Chainalysis as the compliance foundation for its digital asset platform. Calgary Police Service became the first police agency in Canada to create a dedicated blockchain investigation team in partnership with Chainalysis. The site also describes IRS-CI, a 2,000-agent federal agency, using Chainalysis to investigate and prosecute crypto financial crimes.

paragraphs: Miller Mendel, Inc. creates, sells and supports software for city, county, state and federal public safety agencies. Its first and flagship product, eSOPH, is a cloud-based system for public agencies that must run in-depth pre-employment background investigations on their applicants. Since 2011 its customers have been city police departments, county sheriff's offices, state police agencies, district attorney's offices and other criminal justice entities.

The company says eSOPH has been credited with cutting the time to process a background investigation by more than 50%, so applicants can be hired more quickly. Partnerships with Experian and Fama Technologies add one-click retrieval of credit reports and of social media and online activity reports. A captain at the Riverside County Sheriff's Department in California, which conducts over 2,500 applicant investigations a year, estimates a 50% time saving per investigation.

Miller Mendel describes itself as a minority owned, small business. It reports serving over 16,000 agency users. More than 90% of new clients, it says, come by referral from existing eSOPH users. In April 2026 NEOGOV, a workforce management platform built for the public sector, announced it had acquired Miller Mendel and was bringing eSOPH into its public safety software portfolio. The release said eSOPH was used by more than 300 customers, including some of the largest law enforcement agencies in the country.

paragraphs: Guardian Alliance Technologies sells background investigation software built for law enforcement agencies, fire departments and other public safety agencies. The company describes it as an end-to-end background investigation solution that gives agencies a way to pre-screen, investigate and approve applicants. It is sold on monthly and annual plans. The site says over 1,500 agencies nationwide use it.

The process starts with a quick assessment of each applicant to decide whether a full investigation should be conducted. From there, a centralized data center stores an applicant's job-seeking activity, such as the agencies they have applied to. That record gives investigators access to all applicant answers provided to any agency in the Guardian Alliance. Access to the National Decertification Index is a free, standard part of the Triage Center, which the company says helps agencies identify decertified applicants.

Guardian states that it complies with the FBI CJIS Security Policy. President and founder Justin Biedinger describes ten years on patrol and 3 years as a background investigator before the tools were built. He says the tools mimic existing background processes while giving investigators more efficient means to do their job. A June 2022 news item announces the addition of more than 80 new law enforcement agencies since the start of that year.

brands.description: The former name of EverDriven. Palladium Equity Partners announced on 2 March 2020 that it had acquired ALC Schools, LLC and Red Rock Technology, LLC - combined, 'ALC', 'a mission-driven provider of alternative transportation solutions' (palladiumequity.com/media/, read 2026-09-02). alcschools.com now answers HTTP 301 straight to www.everdriven.com, verified 2026-09-02; the destination refuses an identified crawler with 403 but a browser lands on EverDriven. There is no separate ALC Schools site, board or booth: this is one company under two names, not a parent and a subsidiary. It sat in the blocked queue as 'we learned nothing' because a 403'd probe cannot follow a redirect.

notes.text: Website verified 2026-08-25 by an independent check that was asked to reject it. Page says: "Revolutionizing offender GPS monitoring with innovative technology and unmatched reliability to drive positive social impact." Fetched https://geo-satis.com. The page is branded GEOSATIS and the quoted line ties it to offender monitoring for justice agencies. Hardware matches the 'ankle device' description specifically: the named products are the ODIN-i GPS bracelet, a Beacon RF transmitter for home-curfew monitoring, and a Victim App for proximity alerts — this is electronic monitoring for courts/corrections, not a same-name firm in another sector. The Swiss attribution is supported on-page by a Swiss flag mark in the footer alongside '© 2025 GEOSATIS All Rights Reserved', though the page does not print an HQ address in so many words; the Swiss claim is the weakest element of the description, while the substantive claim (electronic monitoring devices for justice agencies) is solidly evidenced. Own primary domain, no redirect, no parent-domain issue.
